definition: Open disagreement with an opinion or decision that most people or those in charge accept.
example: Despite some dissent among the staff, the restaurant switched to a shorter menu.
nuance: Dissent is disagreement voiced against a majority or an authority; ordinary disagreement can be private or between equals.
prompt: A science club votes on which project to build for the school fair.
options: Only one member voiced dissent, arguing that a volcano model had been done too many times.
Everyone nodded happily in dissent, so the volcano model was approved without objection.
The club cheered the dissent of their weather balloon as it drifted slowly back to the field.
The members agreed the finished poster looked dissent enough to hang in the hallway.
reasons: A lone member objecting to the group's choice is exactly a case of open disagreement.
Happy nodding and approval with no objection show agreement, the reverse of the word's meaning.
This confuses the word with its look-alike descent, which means a downward movement.
The word is a noun about disagreeing, not the adjective decent, meaning acceptable.

practice.prompt: A choir director announces the song the group will perform at the spring concert.
options: The sopranos practiced a slow dissent down the scale, from the highest note to the lowest.
The director gave her dissent, so the students were finally allowed to leave rehearsal early.
When the tenors expressed dissent, the director agreed to hear their case for another song.
The choir showed its dissent by cheerfully accepting every song the director picked.
reasons: Moving downward through notes is a descent; the look-alike has been swapped in.
Granting permission is consent or assent; the word here wrongly means approval.
The tenors push back against the leader's choice, which is what the word describes.
Cheerful acceptance of every choice is compliance, not objection.
